prompt: Does there exist a prime $p$ and distinct positive integers $y_1,y_2,y_3$ with $y_i<\frac p3$ for each $1\le i\le 3$ and $y_1^3\equiv y_2^3\equiv y_3^3 \pmod p$? Answer Yes or No (and prove it).
acceptedAnswers: No, there is no such prime

solutions.title: Cube roots of unity
solutions.body:
Suppose such $p,y_1,y_2,y_3$ exist. Since $0<y_i<p/3<p$, each $y_i$ is invertible mod $p$. Put $u=y_2y_1^{-1}$ and $v=y_3y_1^{-1}$. Then $u^3\equiv v^3\equiv 1$ and $u,v,1$ are distinct mod $p$ because $y_1,y_2,y_3$ are distinct residues.

Since $x^3-1=(x-1)(x^2+x+1)$ and $\mathbb Z/p$ is a field, $u$ and $v$ are roots of $x^2+x+1$ different from each other. A quadratic has at most two roots, so $u,v$ are exactly the two roots and by Vieta $u+v\equiv -1\pmod p$.

Multiplying by $y_1$: $y_2+y_3\equiv -y_1$, i.e. $y_1+y_2+y_3\equiv 0\pmod p$.

But $0<y_1+y_2+y_3<3\cdot\frac p3=p$, so the sum is strictly between $0$ and $p$ and cannot be divisible by $p$. Contradiction.

**Answer: No.**

prompt: The $n$ vertices of a regular $n$-gon are drawn, and each of the $\binom n2$ edges between them is colored such that no two edges of the same color intersect at a point which is not a vertex of the $n$-gon. What is the minimum number of different colors that can be used to color all the edges? (Give the answer as a function of $n\ge 4$, with proof.)

solutions.title: Lower bound
solutions.body:
For even $n=2m\ge4$ the $m$ diameters pairwise cross at the centre, so they need $m=n/2$ different colors.

For odd $n=2m+1\ge5$ take the $n$ longest diagonals $\{i,i+m\}$ (indices mod $n$). Two of them $\{i,i+m\}$, $\{j,j+m\}$ with $d=j-i \bmod n$ share an endpoint exactly when $d\in\{m,m+1\}$ and otherwise their endpoints interleave, so they cross. Hence two diagonals of the same color must share an endpoint, so they are neighbours in the cycle formed by these $n$ diagonals (each has exactly two neighbours). A cycle of length $n\ge5$ has no three pairwise adjacent members, so a color class has at most $2$ of them and at least $\lceil n/2\rceil$ colors are needed.

solutions.title: Construction
solutions.body:
Label the vertices $0,1,\dots,n-1$ around the polygon and give each chord $\{i,j\}$ its *sum* $i+j \bmod n$. Put the chords with sums $\{2k,2k+1\}$ into class $k$ ($k=0,1,\dots$).

Each class is the edge set of a zigzag path $0,1,-1,2,-2,\dots$ (shifted by $k$): its edges have sums $1,0,1,0,\dots$. This path is non-crossing: at each step the visited vertices form a block of consecutive vertices and the new edge joins the current end of the block to the vertex just outside its other end; all earlier vertices lie on one side of this chord and all later ones on the other side (or on it), so no two edges of the path cross.

For $n=2m$ the classes $k=0,\dots,m-1$ use sums $\{0,1\},\{2,3\},\dots,\{n-2,n-1\}$, which are all $n$ sums, so every chord is colored with $m=n/2$ colors.

For $n=2m+1$ the classes $k=0,\dots,m-1$ use the sums $0,\dots,2m-1$ and the remaining chords all have sum $2m$; they are parallel, hence non-crossing, and get one more color. Total $m+1=\lceil n/2\rceil$.

**Answer: $\lceil n/2\rceil$** (for $n\le3$ no two edges cross and one color suffices).

prompt: Let $p$ be a prime and let $S$ be the set of positive integers $m>1$ such that the only positive divisors of $m$ that are congruent to $1 \pmod p$ are $1$ and $m$ (so in particular $m\equiv1\pmod p$). Suppose some $m\in S$ has exactly $p-1$ distinct prime factors. Show that $m=q_1\cdots q_{p-1}$ for distinct primes $q_1,\dots,q_{p-1}$ with $q_1\equiv\cdots\equiv q_{p-1}\pmod p$.
answer: Proof: $m$ is squarefree and all its prime factors are congruent mod $p$

solutions.title: Squarefree
solutions.body:
Since $m\equiv1 \pmod p$, $p\nmid m$. Write $m=\prod_{i=1}^{p-1}q_i^{e_i}$ with $e_i\ge1$ and $N=\sum e_i\ge p-1$. Multiply the primes one at a time to get a chain $1=d_0\mid d_1\mid\dots\mid d_N=m$ (each $d_{t+1}/d_t$ prime).

If $d_s\equiv d_t\pmod p$ with $0\le s<t\le N-1$, then $d_s$ is invertible mod $p$ so the divisor $d_t/d_s$ of $m$ is $\equiv1$; it is neither $1$ nor $m$ (it is $>1$, and $<m$ since $d_t<m$). This contradicts $m\in S$. So $d_0,\dots,d_{N-1}$ are $N$ distinct nonzero residues mod $p$, which forces $N\le p-1$. Hence $N=p-1$, all $e_i=1$, $m=q_1\cdots q_{p-1}$ with distinct primes, and $d_0,\dots,d_{p-2}$ run through **all** nonzero residues mod $p$ exactly once.

solutions.title: The primes are congruent
solutions.body:
Let $g$ be a primitive root mod $p$ and write $q_i\equiv g^{a_i}$. Partial products $d_t=q_1\cdots q_t$ ($0\le t\le p-2$) correspond to exponents $s_t=a_1+\dots+a_t$, and by the previous step $\{s_0,\dots,s_{p-2}\}$ is a complete residue system mod $p-1$, with $s_0=0$. Also no $a_i\equiv0$ (else $q_i\equiv1$ is a divisor of $m$ other than $1,m$).

Suppose not all $a_i$ are congruent mod $p-1$; after reordering the primes, $a_1\not\equiv a_2$. The residue $a_2\not\equiv0$ is hit by some $s_x$ with $1\le x\le p-2$, and $x\ne1$ because $s_1=a_1\not\equiv a_2$. Then $s_x-a_2=a_1+a_3+\dots+a_x\equiv0$, i.e. $q_1q_3q_4\cdots q_x\equiv1\pmod p$. This is a divisor of $m$ that is not $1$ (nonempty product) and not $m$ (it omits $q_2$), contradicting $m\in S$.

Hence $a_1\equiv a_2\equiv\dots\equiv a_{p-1}\pmod{p-1}$, i.e. $q_1\equiv\dots\equiv q_{p-1}\pmod p$. ∎

prompt: In triangle $ABC$, points $E$ and $F$ are chosen on sides $AC$ and $AB$ respectively such that $AE=AF$. Point $K$ is on segment $EF$ such that $AK$, $BE$ and $CF$ intersect at a point, and points $B'$ and $C'$ are on lines $AC$ and $AB$ such that $BB'\parallel CK$ and $CC'\parallel BK$. Points $U$ and $V$ are on the line through $A$ parallel to $EF$ such that $UC=UC'$ and $VB=VB'$. Prove that $AU=AV$.

solutions.title: Coordinates
solutions.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$ and let the bisector of $\angle A$ be the $y$-axis, with $\theta=\tfrac12\angle A$, $s=\sin\theta$, $c=\cos\theta$. Then $AB$, $AC$ have directions $(-s,c)$, $(s,c)$. Write $B=\beta(-s,c)$, $C=\gamma(s,c)$, $F=f(-s,c)$, $E=f(s,c)$ (as $AE=AF=f$, with $\beta>f$, $\gamma>f$), and $K=(k,fc)$ on $EF$, so $FK=k+fs$ and $EK=fs-k$. Since $EF$ is horizontal, the line through $A$ parallel to $EF$ is the $x$-axis.

Let $C'=\lambda(-s,c)$ on line $AB$. $CC'\parallel BK$ means $(C'-C)\times(K-B)=0$ with $C'-C=(-s(\lambda+\gamma),c(\lambda-\gamma))$, $K-B=(k+\beta s,c(f-\beta))$:
$$s(\lambda+\gamma)(\beta-f)=(\lambda-\gamma)(k+\beta s)\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda=\frac{\gamma(k+2\beta s-sf)}{sf+k},\quad \gamma-\lambda=\frac{2s\gamma(f-\beta)}{sf+k}.$$
(The denominator $sf+k=FK>0$.)

For $U=(u,0)$, $UC=UC'$ gives $(u-\gamma s)^2+\gamma^2c^2=(u+\lambda s)^2+\lambda^2c^2$, i.e. $2us(\gamma+\lambda)=\gamma^2-\lambda^2$, so $u=\dfrac{\gamma-\lambda}{2s}$ (note $\gamma+\lambda\neq0$: $\gamma+\lambda=0$ would force $k=-s\beta<-sf$, impossible for $K$ on segment $EF$). Therefore
$$AU=|u|=\frac{\gamma(\beta-f)}{FK}=\frac{AC\cdot BF}{FK}.$$
By the mirror symmetry $x\mapsto-x$ (which swaps $B\leftrightarrow C$, $E\leftrightarrow F$), $AV=\dfrac{AB\cdot CE}{EK}$.

solutions.title: Ceva and the ratio lemma
solutions.body:
Let $AK$ meet $BC$ at $P$. Ceva in $ABC$ (cevians $AP,BE,CF$) with $AE=AF$ gives $\dfrac{BP}{PC}=\dfrac{FB}{AF}\cdot\dfrac{AE}{EC}=\dfrac{BF}{CE}$.

The ratio lemma in triangles $ABC$ and $AFE$ (same cevian $AP$, so the same angles at $A$) gives $\dfrac{BP}{PC}=\dfrac{AB\sin\angle BAP}{AC\sin\angle PAC}$ and $\dfrac{FK}{KE}=\dfrac{AF\sin\angle FAK}{AE\sin\angle KAE}=\dfrac{\sin\angle BAP}{\sin\angle PAC}$. Hence $\dfrac{FK}{KE}=\dfrac{BP}{PC}\cdot\dfrac{AC}{AB}=\dfrac{BF\cdot AC}{CE\cdot AB}$, i.e. $\dfrac{AC\cdot BF}{FK}=\dfrac{AB\cdot CE}{EK}$.

So $AU=AV$. ∎

prompt: Let $\mathbb Q$ denote the set of rational numbers. Suppose $f:\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q$ is a function that satisfies $0<|f(x)-f(y)|\le|x-y|$ for all $x\ne y\in\mathbb Q$. Must $f$ be monotonic? (A function $f$ is increasing if $f(x)<f(y)$ whenever $x<y$. A function $f$ is monotonic if either $f$ or $-f$ is increasing.) Answer Yes or No (and prove it).
acceptedAnswers: No, f need not be monotonic

solutions.title: A counterexample
solutions.body:
Let $x_0=3-2\sqrt2\approx0.172$ and define on $\mathbb R$
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac12\Big(\dfrac1{1+x}\Big)^2,&x\ge x_0,\\[2mm] \dfrac14\Big(\dfrac1{1-x}\Big)^2,&x\le x_0.\end{cases}$$
Both formulas agree at $x_0$ ($1+x_0=4-2\sqrt2$, $1-x_0=2\sqrt2-2$, and $\frac12(4-2\sqrt2)^{-2}=\frac14(2\sqrt2-2)^{-2}=\frac1{48-32\sqrt2}$), so $f$ is continuous. Clearly $f(x)\in\mathbb Q$ for rational $x$.

**Lipschitz.** For $x>x_0$: $|f'(x)|=(1+x)^{-3}\le(4-2\sqrt2)^{-3}<1.17^{-3}<1$. For $x<x_0$: $f'(x)=\frac12(1-x)^{-3}\le\frac12(2\sqrt2-2)^{-3}<\frac12(0.8)^{-3}<0.98$. So $|f'|<1$ on both pieces and $f$ is continuous, hence $|f(x)-f(y)|\le|x-y|$ for all real $x,y$ (mean value theorem on each side of $x_0$, and the triangle inequality through $x_0$).

**Injective on $\mathbb Q$.** $f$ is strictly increasing on $(-\infty,x_0)$ and strictly decreasing on $(x_0,\infty)$, so $f(r)\ne f(s)$ if $r,s$ lie on the same side. If $r<x_0<s$ were rational with $f(r)=f(s)$, then $\frac14(1-r)^{-2}=\frac12(1+s)^{-2}$, i.e. $\big(\frac{1+s}{1-r}\big)^2=2$, so $\sqrt2$ would be rational. Impossible. Thus $0<|f(x)-f(y)|\le|x-y|$ for all rationals $x\ne y$.

**Not monotonic.** $f$ is strictly increasing on rationals below $x_0$ (so $-f$ is not increasing) and strictly decreasing on rationals above $x_0$ (so $f$ is not increasing).

**Answer: No.**

prompt: Let $a,b,c,d$ be positive integers such that $ab=c^2+d$, $2c\mid a-b$, and $cd<a-b$. Prove that $d$ is a perfect square.
answer: Proof by Pell-type descent: $x^2-(k^2+1)c^2=d$ forces $d$ to be a square

solutions.title: Reduce to a Pell-type equation
solutions.body:
Since $cd<a-b$, $a>b$; write $a-b=2ck$ with $k\ge1$ an integer. Then $a+b\equiv a-b\equiv0\pmod 2$; write $a+b=2x$. From $(a+b)^2=(a-b)^2+4ab$:
$$x^2=c^2k^2+c^2+d,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad x^2-(k^2+1)c^2=d.\tag{1}$$
Also $cd<2ck$ gives $d<2k$. Fix $k$ and $d$ (so $d<2k\le k^2+1$).

solutions.title: Descent
solutions.body:
If $(x,c)$ with $x,c\ge0$ solves (1), so does
$$x'=(2k^2+1)x-2k(k^2+1)c,\qquad c'=(2k^2+1)c-2kx,$$
since $(2k^2+1)^2-4k^2(k^2+1)=1$ (multiplication by the unit $(2k^2+1)+2k\sqrt{k^2+1}$ of norm $1$); both are integers.

*Claim: if $c\ge k$ then $|c'|<c$.* From (1), $x>kc$, so $c'<c\iff 2k^2c<2kx\iff kc<x$, true. And $c'>-c\iff (k^2+1)c>kx\iff (k^2+1)^2c^2>k^2x^2=k^2(k^2+1)c^2+k^2d\iff(k^2+1)c^2>k^2d$, true because $c\ge k$ and $d<k^2+1$.

*Claim: (1) has no solution with $0<c<k$.* Then $k^2c^2<x^2=k^2c^2+c^2+d<(kc+1)^2$, because $c^2+d<c^2+2k\le2kc+1$ (equivalent to $(c-1)(c+1-2k)\le0$, true for $1\le c\le 2k-1$). A square strictly between consecutive squares is impossible.

Start from our solution $(x,c)$ with $c\ge1$ and replace $(x,c)$ by $(|x'|,|c'|)$ while $c\ge k$; $c$ strictly decreases, so after finitely many steps $c<k$, and by the second claim $c=0$. Then (1) reads $x^2=d$ with $x$ an integer. Hence $d$ is a perfect square. ∎

prompt: Puddles the Frog has a row of $n\ge2$ lilypads, labeled $1$ through $n$, with $1$ unit between consecutive lilypads. He is at lilypad $1$ and wishes to visit lilypads $2$ through $n$ once each, before ending up back at lilypad $1$. However, he may jump no more than $3$ units at a time. Let $f(n)$ be the maximum total distance of Puddles's trip, starting from lilypad $1$ and ending back at lilypad $1$. Determine, with proof, the value of $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{f(n)}{n}$.

solutions.title: Reformulation and local structure
solutions.body:
The trip is a Hamiltonian cycle on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with edges of length $\le3$, and its length is $\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}c_i$ where $c_i$ is the number of jumps crossing the gap between $i$ and $i+1$. Each $c_i$ is even and $\ge2$ (a closed tour crosses a cut an even, positive number of times). The jumps across gap $i$ join $\{i-2,i-1,i\}$ to $\{i+1,i+2,i+3\}$; the left ends are $i-2$ (at most 1 jump, to $i+1$), $i-1$ (at most 2), $i$ (at most 2), so $c_i\le5$, hence $c_i\in\{2,4\}$. Also $c_1=c_{n-1}=2$.

If $c_i=4$, deleting the crossing jumps splits the cycle into 2 'left runs' (paths in $\{1..i\}$ covering all left vertices) and 2 right runs; a vertex with two crossing jumps is a run by itself.

**Lemma.** If $3\le i\le n-3$ and $c_i=4$, then the tour uses the jumps $(i-2,i+1),(i-1,i+2),(i,i+3)$.

*Proof.* If $(i-2,i+1)$ is missing, the four left ends come from $i-1$ and $i$ only, so both are one-vertex left runs, and the two left runs would cover only $\{i-1,i\}$, but $i-2\ge1$ is also a left vertex. Contradiction; symmetrically $(i,i+3)$ is used. If $(i-1,i+2)$ is missing, the four left ends must be $i-2$ (jump to $i+1$), $i-1$ (jump to $i+1$), and two at $i$; the jump $(i,i+3)$ is one of them, so $i$ is a one-vertex left run, while $i+1$ has both its jumps crossing. Then $i-2\to i+1\to i-1$ together with the other left run (a path from $i-1$ to $i-2$) forms a closed cycle missing vertex $i$, contradiction. ∎

So a gap with $c_i=4$ uses the three length-3 jumps above plus exactly one more crossing jump, which is one of $(i-1,i+1),(i,i+1),(i,i+2)$.

solutions.title: Upper bound
solutions.body:
**Claim.** If $3\le i<j\le n-3$, $c_i=c_j=4$, then $j-i\notin\{2,3\}$.

If $j=i+2$ or $i+3$, then $i+1$ has the jumps $(i-2,i+1)$ (from gap $i$) and $(i+1,i+4)$ (from gap $j$), and $i+2$ has $(i-1,i+2)$ and $(i+2,i+5)$; both vertices already have two jumps. But the fourth crossing jump of gap $i$ is $(i-1,i+1)$, $(i,i+1)$ or $(i,i+2)$, giving $i+1$ or $i+2$ a third jump. Contradiction.

Hence any two interior gaps with $c=4$ differ by $1$ or by at least $4$, so among any $5$ consecutive gaps at most $2$ have $c=4$ (three would have to be consecutive, but then two of them differ by 2). With $m=n-5$ interior gaps there are at most $2\lceil m/5\rceil\le \frac{2m}5+2$ fours there, plus at most $2$ from the gaps $2$ and $n-2$. So the number of fours is $\le\frac{2n}5+2$ and
$$f(n)\le2(n-1)+2\Big(\frac{2n}5+2\Big)=\frac{14n}{5}+2.$$

solutions.title: Lower bound (construction)
solutions.body:
For $n=10k$ ($k\ge2$) take the cycle
$$1,3,6,9,\ \underbrace{10j+7,\,10j+10,\,10j+13,\,10j+16,\,10j+19}_{j=0,1,\dots,k-2},\ n-3,\ n,\ n-2,\ n-5,\ n-8,\ \underbrace{10j+4,\,10j+1,\,10j-2,\,10j-5,\,10j-8}_{j=k-1,\dots,1},\ 4,\ \text{(back to }1).$$
Every lilypad appears exactly once and all jumps are $2$ or $3$ (the jumps are $1\to3$: $2$; $3\to6\to9$: $3,3$; inside each block $9\to7$, $19\to17$ etc. are $2$ and the four steps of the block are $3$; $10k-1\to n-3\to n\to n-2$: $2,3,2$; $n-2\to n-5\to n-8$: $3,3$; then the backward blocks, entered by jumps of $2$; finally $2\to4\to1$: $2,3$). Its length is $8+14(k-1)+13+14(k-1)+5=28k-2=\frac{14n}5-2$.

For any $n$, from an optimal tour on $n$ lilypads we can add lilypad $n+1$: the two jumps at $n$ go to distinct lilypads $\ge n-3$, so one of them, $(u,n)$, has $u\ge n-2$; replace it by $u\to n+1\to n$ (allowed, since $n+1-u\le3$), which lengthens the tour by $2$. So $f(n+1)\ge f(n)+2$, and for $n=10k+r$ ($0\le r<10$): $f(n)\ge28k-2+2r\ge\frac{14n}5-10$.

Therefore $\frac{14n}5-10\le f(n)\le\frac{14n}5+2$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{f(n)}n=\frac{14}{5}$.

**Answer: $\frac{14}5$.**
